title: Mina and the Rust Buster
markdown:
Sunlight streamed into the shed. Mina felt a jolt of excitement. Today was the day. Professor Imani needed her for an urgent retrieval: critical batteries in an old automaton.

Mina zipped her jacket. The shed door creaked open. The automaton sat, a rusty knight. Flint the fox padded in. “Rust? That’s a tough lock!”

Mina tapped the battery compartment. Jammed. “Professor Imani said it’s oxidised. The metal’s stuck.” She tugged. Nothing. Flint tried gnawing. “No good,” he grumbled.

Then Mina’s eyes spotted it: a beaker with brilliant sky-blue liquid. “Professor Imani’s copper sulfate.” She remembered a lesson: iron reacts. Old nails in a puddle turned orange. Iron lost electrons. Oxidation. Could she do the opposite? Make the oxide give way?

“Flint,” she whispered, “what if we used this blue stuff to watch the electrons move?”

Mina poured the blue liquid into a pan. She tossed in scrap metal — bent nails, a rusty bolt. She watched, breath held. The blue swirled, clouding. Copper began to ghost onto the iron. The nails roughened. “It’s happening. The iron is oxidising — losing electrons. The copper ions are gaining them. Reduction. Two sides of the same conversation.”

Flint watched, fascinated, as the blue faded toward brown. A chemical dance, yes. But the automaton’s rust was iron oxide, already oxidised. Dumping copper sulfate on a rusty knight would not kindly un-rust it. It would give the iron more reason to dissolve.

Mina’s coding mind flipped the logic. Oxidation is loss. Reduction is gain. To loosen rust, she needed the oxide to be reduced, or dissolved, not a new metal plated on top. She mixed a mild acid bath — vinegar, a pinch of salt as electrolyte — and set the casing in it, connecting a small workshop cell so the rusty iron sat as the place electrons could arrive. Tiny bubbles rose, like escaping pearls. The angry red rust softened, lifted, peeled.

After tense minutes, Mina lifted the casing. The metal gleamed, remarkably clean. The screws turned with a satisfying click. Pop. The compartment sprang open, revealing two shining batteries.

Professor Imani arrived, her face breaking into a wide smile. “Remarkable, Mina. You saw a chemical conversation.”

Mina beamed. “The copper sulfate showed me the two directions. Oxidation is losing electrons. Reduction is gaining. The rust had already lost. I had to give a path back — or a way for the oxide to let go. Redox.”

“Precisely. You applied redox reactions. You used your coding mind to decode a chemical puzzle.”

Flint nudged a battery, wonder in his foxy eyes. “So rust can be un-rusted?”

“Sometimes,” Professor Imani said. “If you know which way the electrons need to go.”

Mina slid the batteries free. The knight’s chest was open, honest metal showing. Flint sat in the stripe of sun, and the blue beaker, having taught its lesson, stayed on the bench where it belonged.
